name: Northern Pomo
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 4 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: O'Connor, Mary Catherine. 1987. Topics in Northern Pomo Grammar. PhD dissertation, University of California, Berkeley. xi+339 pp. (eScholarship item 09r209d2; published 1992, New York: Garland).
catalog_locator: Diss. pp. 9-10 with fn. 4, Ch. 1 sec. 3.1.1 'Phonology' (the quote's final clause 'syllable of the main verb.' is the first line of p. 10); diss. p. 20, Ch. 2 sec. 2.2 'The root'. File; pages rendered with page render and read as images; scan transcript of pp. 25-27 and 37
catalog_quote: Vowels in unaccented syllables are laxed. Vihman (1976) analyzes Northern Pomo as a language in which "stress is an inherent lexical feature, and pitch variation is a phonetic phenomenon correlated with syllable structure" (1976:77). Vowel length is virtually always accompanied by low pitch. There are a few examples where vowel length is not accompanied by low pitch, but these are largely loan words like sapa:ta, 'shoes'. ... I have found evidence of stress realized through neither pitch nor length, but amplitude.[4] In addition, there are subtle pitch alternations associated with at least interrogative and imperative voice. Both of these are marked by a distinct falling pitch on the last syllable of the main verb. [fn. 4] As reported in Chapter Two, the root of a verb stem usually bears the stress. Aside from this general observation, I have not yet worked out all the realizations of stress and pitch accent at the word, phrase and sentence level in sufficient detail to be able to include transcriptions of prosodic phenomena here. [p. 20, sec. 2.2 The root] The root is usually of the form CV. ... (13) ma-bah "to kick, to strike with the foot" / pha-bah "to punch, to strike with the hand" The root typically carries the accent. The rules of phonetic realization of accent have not yet been worked out.
world_status: statement found in an open source

Vihman (1976) analyzes Northern Pomo as a language in which \"stress is an inherent lexical feature, and pitch variation is a phonetic phenomenon correlated with syllable structure\"…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress/accent is treated as lexical (not positionally predictable), following Vihman 1976; in verbs it typically falls on the root syllable, i.e. the CV(:) root that follows an optional CV- instrumental prefix (hence commonly the second syllable of prefixed verb stems). Long vowels carry low pitch; unaccented vowels are laxed; amplitude is reported as a stress correlate independent of pitch and length.
new_statements.exceptions: 'usually'/'typically' on the root; loanwords like sapa:ta 'shoes' have length without low pitch; author states the phonetic realization of accent and its word/phrase/sentence-level behaviour were not worked out and prosody is not transcribed in the dissertation.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level (verb stem) generalization; interrogative and imperative carry a falling pitch on the last syllable of the main verb (sentence-level). The dedicated primary treatment is Vihman 1976 (pitch accent analysis), which O'Connor defers to.
new_statements.identity_note: O'Connor's data are from one speaker, Edna Campbell Guerrero, largely in the dialect of the balo?khay pho?ma? group (Potter Valley / Calpella area), per diss. p. 7; language-level Northern Pomo (nort2966, ISO pej). Vihman's 1960s work was with the same speaker.

new_statements.quote: Pn, Pc, Pne and Pe have a phonemic accent that occurs mostly on the first or second syllable of a word. It is primarily a pitch accent (tone) in Pn and stress in Pc, Pne, and Pe. [...] Halpern (ms.) suggests the same pattern of partial morphological predictability also exists in Pn, Pc and Pne. [...] according to Halpern, the position of the Pn tone is partially conditioned by the structure of the syllable on which it occurs: closed syllables seem to take precedence over light ones and syllables closed by /·/ do not occur with tone (high tone in Vihman's recordings), just as in Pk, the only other Pomo language in which the prosodic accent also involves pitch rather than stress.

new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the catalog record (O'Connor 1987: lexical accent, 'the root of a verb stem usually bears the stress', classification morphological): McLendon likewise reports a phonemic accent with partial morphological (root) predictability per Halpern, and adds placement detail (mostly 1st or 2nd syllable; syllable-structure conditioning: closed syllables preferred, length-closed syllables toneless) and diachrony. It differs on the NATURE of the accent: McLendon (1971, from Vihman's and Halpern's field data) calls the Pn accent 'primarily a pitch accent (tone)', whereas O'Connor, following Vihman 1976, treats stress as the inherent lexical feature and pitch as phonetically conditioned by…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Northern Pomo (Pn) has a phonemic (lexically contrastive) word accent, realized primarily as pitch (tone: high vs low tone in Vihman's transcription) rather than stress, falling mostly on the first or second syllable of the word; following Halpern (ms.) its location is partly morphologically predictable (root accent, as in Eastern Pomo verbs) and partly conditioned by syllable structure: closed syllables take the tone in preference to light ones, and syllables closed by length /·/ do not carry tone. Diachronically (sec. 135, p. 38) Pn preserved the phonemic Proto-Pomo accent; deletion of pre-tonic syllables beginning in *ʔ or *h turned many second-syllable accents into initial accents.
new_statements.secondary_stress: none stated for Northern Pomo (a 'secondary accent' is mentioned only for two reconstructed Proto-Pomo compounds, ASHES and TEARS, typescript p. 37)
new_statements.exceptions: accent 'mostly' on the first or second syllable (not exclusively); syllables closed by length do not take tone; nouns give no synchronic basis for identifying roots (stated for Pe, extended by Halpern to Pn)
new_statements.identity_note: McLendon's Pn = Northern Pomo as recorded by Eero Vihman (phonemic transcription, Ch. II p. 9) with A. M. Halpern's notes; no dialect named. O'Connor 1987 (catalog) describes Northern Pomo of her own fieldwork (1980s speakers).

sources.note: Sec. 3.1.1 Phonology (p. 9): follows Vihman (1976:77) that 'stress is an inherent lexical feature' with pitch a phonetic correlate of syllable structure (long vowels carry low pitch); vowels in unaccented syllables are laxed; fn. 4: 'the root of a verb stem usually bears the stress'; prosody not otherwise worked out and not transcribed. Sec. 2.2 (p. 20): 'The root typically carries the accent.' (root = CV(:) following an optional CV- instrumental prefix).
